climate_context.source: NASA POWER Daily Point API (AG Community)

limitations: Decision-support model only; does not provide guaranteed yield, profit, or water delivery certainty.
Recommendations rely on NASA POWER gridded satellite reanalysis (~0.5° × 0.625° resolution) which does not capture hyper-local field microtopography or soil salinity patches.
Actual performance depends on physical canal rotation schedules (warabandi) and tube-well electrical grid reliability in Peshawar Valley.
general_assumptions: Farm retains functional tube-well irrigation with medium seasonal reliability.
Soil texture is loamy with moderate infiltration and organic matter ~0.6-0.8%.
Agronomic practices follow Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Agriculture Extension standard seedbed preparation.

scenarios.title: Conventional Cereal Monoculture (Wheat – Maize)
scenarios.description: Standard two-season cereal rotation prevalent across Peshawar and Charsadda districts, balancing food security with familiar local marketing channels.

seasonal_calendar.water_notes: Requires 4-5 irrigations; crown root initiation and grain fill are critical moisture stages.
High water requirement coinciding with peak summer temperatures (36-41°C) and monsoon.

rationale: Aligns with Peshawar Valley's most established grain supply chains and local household consumption.
Both crops have documented heat tolerance thresholds matching NASA POWER historical temperature regimes.
benefits: Reliable local cash and fodder markets with negligible adoption barrier for farm labor.
Allows utilization of standard mechanized threshing and seed drill equipment.
risks: Heavy synthetic nitrogen fertilizer dependence depletes soil biological activity over time.
High water demand during June-July peak temperatures stresses tube-well groundwater pumping.
assumptions: Assumes reliable electricity or diesel availability for tube-well during peak June heat waves.

scenarios.title: Nitrogen-Fixing Pulse Diversification (Wheat – Mung Bean)
scenarios.description: Introduces short-duration mung bean in early kharif/zaid window to break continuous cereal deplete cycles, fix atmospheric nitrogen, and reduce peak summer water demand.

seasonal_calendar.water_notes: Benefits from residual soil nitrogen left by preceding pulse cycle.
Low water demand; requires only 2-3 light irrigations compared to heavy maize flooding.

rationale: Short duration (70 days) fits neatly between wheat harvest and late summer, lowering irrigation volume during peak June evaporative demand.
Rhizobium biological nitrogen fixation enriches topsoil organic nitrogen, dampening synthetic urea requirements.
benefits: Substantial water conservation during critical June heat spells identified in NASA POWER climate data.
Diversifies farm income with high-value edible pulse grain commanding premium market prices in Peshawar.
risks: Pods are susceptible to shattering and flower drop if unseasonal intense monsoon rains hit during early July ripening.
Requires certified rhizobium inoculant and careful aphid monitoring.
assumptions: Assumes seedbed drainage is sufficient to prevent standing water during monsoon cloudbursts.

scenarios.title: Soil Health & Multi-Cut Forage Cover (Berseem Clover – Maize)
scenarios.description: Replaces continuous grain cereals with Berseem clover in rabi to produce high-protein livestock forage, provide continuous ground canopy cover, and aggressively regenerate depleted valley soils.

seasonal_calendar.water_notes: Requires frequent shallow irrigations; high water use efficiency due to continuous vegetative cover.
Grows vigorously on clover-enriched nitrogen residual, improving water retention in root zone.

rationale: Dense legume canopy suppresses winter weed proliferation and dramatically enhances soil organic matter in loamy soils.
Provides 4 to 6 cuttings of succulent green fodder for Peshawar Valley peri-urban dairy herds.
benefits: Exceptional soil structure, microbial biomass, and nitrogen enrichment.
Steady weekly cash flow from green forage sales in Peshawar livestock markets.
risks: Requires access to livestock or established local green forage market routes.
Frequent cutting requires sustained farm labor availability from December through April.
assumptions: Assumes farm labor or local peri-urban fodder buyer handles regular bi-weekly forage harvesting.
